introduction-the-reshuffling-nightmare.core: Placing keys with `hash(key) % N` spreads them evenly, but changing N moves almost every key: going from 4 to 5 servers remaps about 80% of keys. For caches that means a stampede of misses; for databases a massive data migration. Consistent hashing changes the mapping so adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys.

first_principles.problem: Adding one cache server to a cluster of 10 causes a 90% miss rate and overloads the database.
truths: Only the new node's share needs to move.
derivation: Map keys and nodes into the **same space**.

analogy.title: Renumbering every seat when one chair is added
analogy.story: Seating by 'ticket number mod rows' means one extra row reseats the whole theatre.
analogy.breaks: Theatre-goers complain; caches just silently miss.

check.q: Roughly what fraction of keys move when going from N to N+1 with modulo hashing?
check.a: About N/(N+1), nearly all of them, versus the ideal of about 1/(N+1).

the-hash-ring.core: Consistent hashing maps both nodes and keys onto the same circular space (for example 0 to 2³²−1). A key belongs to the first node found walking clockwise from its position. Because each node owns only the arc before it, placement depends on neighbours, not on the total node count.

first_principles.problem: An engineer can't see why the ring makes placement independent of N.
truths: Same hash space for keys and nodes.

analogy.title: Bus stops on a circular route
analogy.story: Each passenger boards at the next stop after where they're standing; adding a stop only affects people just before it.
analogy.breaks: Bus stops are evenly spaced by design; hashed nodes land randomly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each node owns the arc ending at it.

points: One circle for keys and nodes.

check.q: Which node owns a key that hashes past the last node on the ring?
check.a: The first node on the ring, because lookup wraps around past the top.

adding-and-removing-nodes.core: When a node joins the ring, it takes over only the keys on the arc between its predecessor and itself, all from one neighbour. When a node leaves, its arc passes to its successor. On average just K/N keys move, and only the adjacent nodes are involved, which keeps scaling and failure recovery cheap.

first_principles.problem: Operators fear scaling out because they expect a cluster-wide rebalance.
truths: Departing node's arc goes to successor.
derivation: On join: **stream keys** from successor for the new arc.

analogy.title: A new shop opening on a high street
analogy.story: It only takes customers from the next shop along, not from every shop in town.
analogy.breaks: Customers choose freely; keys follow the ring rule exactly.

check.q: When a node leaves the ring, which node receives its keys?
check.a: Its clockwise successor, which now owns the merged arc.

the-problem-of-hotspots-and-data-skew.core: With few nodes, random positions on the ring give very uneven arcs: one node may own 40% of the space while another owns 10%. Popular keys add a second skew: a single celebrity key overloads whichever node owns it regardless of arc size. And when a node fails, its whole load lands on one successor, risking cascades.

first_principles.problem: One cache node runs at 90% CPU while others idle, even though the cluster is 'consistently hashed'.
truths: Failover dumps load on one neighbour.

analogy.title: Dividing a pizza by throwing darts
analogy.story: Cut lines at dart marks and some slices are huge, some tiny, and the slice with the pepperoni is everyone's favourite.
analogy.breaks: Pizza doesn't move when a slice is eaten; failed node load cascades.

check.q: Why do virtual nodes not fix a single hot key?
check.a: All traffic for that key still goes to one owner; you need replication, caching or key splitting for that.

virtual-nodes-vnodes-the-solution-to-ske.core: Instead of one position per physical node, give each node many positions (virtual nodes, typically 100–256) on the ring. With many random points the law of large numbers evens out ownership, failover load spreads across many successors, and stronger machines can be given more vnodes for weighted capacity.

first_principles.problem: Plain ring placement leaves arcs uneven and failover overloads one neighbour.
derivation: Keep a **sorted list** of all vnode positions.
Map each vnode to its **physical node**.

analogy.title: Each shop opening many small kiosks across town
analogy.story: Customers spread evenly, and if one shop closes, its kiosks' customers go to many different neighbours.
analogy.breaks: Kiosks cost rent; vnodes cost only ring metadata and more streaming peers.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Ownership spread within a few percent across nodes.

check.q: How do vnodes help when a node fails?
check.a: Its many arcs pass to many different successors, so the extra load spreads across the cluster instead of one neighbour.

real-world-implementations.core: Consistent hashing shows up everywhere: Amazon Dynamo and Cassandra use token rings with vnodes; memcached clients use the Ketama ring; Envoy and NGINX offer ring-hash and Maglev load balancing for session affinity; Discord and Akka shard entities this way. Variants like jump hash and rendezvous (HRW) hashing trade the ring for other placement functions.

first_principles.problem: A team builds custom sharding without realising their proxy already supports consistent hashing.
truths: Variants trade memory, speed, and flexibility.
Proxies often provide it built in.

analogy.title: Different cuisines using the same technique
analogy.story: Braising appears in French, Chinese and Mexican kitchens with local twists; consistent hashing is the same idea with different implementations.
analogy.breaks: Recipes vary by taste; variants vary by measurable trade-offs.

check.q: What advantage does rendezvous hashing have over a ring?
check.a: No ring or vnodes to maintain; each key picks the node with the highest hash(key, node) score, giving even spread with minimal state.

implementation-deep-dive-data-structures.core: A practical ring is a sorted array of (position, node) pairs: lookup is a binary search for the first position ≥ hash(key), O(log(N·V)). Adding or removing a node inserts or removes V entries, O(N·V) with an array or O(V log(N·V)) with a balanced tree. Jump hash needs no storage at all and runs in O(log N), but only supports appending or removing the last bucket.

first_principles.problem: A ring lookup that scans linearly over 50,000 vnodes becomes the proxy's hottest function.
truths: Different structures trade update vs lookup.
derivation: Consider **jump hash** for fixed shard lists.

analogy.title: A phone book vs flipping every page
analogy.story: Sorted names let you open near the right page and halve the search each time.
analogy.breaks: Phone books are reprinted yearly; rings rebuild on every membership change.

branches.label: Alternatives
children: Jump hash O(log N), no memory

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No ring memory; ideal balance; buckets must be numbered 0..n−1.

code.text:
def jump_hash(key: int, buckets: int) -> int:
    b, j = -1, 0
    while j < buckets:
        b = j
        key = (key * 2862933555777941757 + 1) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
        j = int((b + 1) * (1 << 31) / ((key >> 33) + 1))
    return b

check.q: What is jump hash's main limitation?
check.a: Buckets are sequentially numbered, so you can only add or remove at the end, not remove an arbitrary node.
